judgements.reason: stripFlags() stops scanning at the literal `--` token, so no token after it is collected into the `commands` slice; that slice is the only source of subcommand candidates, so `--` is the mechanism that stops later arguments being interpreted as commands.
Find()/innerfind() resolve the target command solely from what stripFlags() returns, which is why the `--` terminator has the effect above.
Corroborates that `--` is a recognised boundary in the parsed argument list, but does not itself state the wrapping procedure.

note: Answer at the pin: put `--` before the arguments. stripFlags() breaks out of its loop on `--`, so tokens after it never reach Find()'s subcommand lookup and are delivered to the command as positional args instead. DisableFlagParsing (command.go:236-238) is a separate, weaker option: it stops flag parsing, not command resolution.

judgements.reason: IsAvailableCommand() is the condition that decides listing in help/usage: a command counts as available if it is runnable OR has available subcommands, so a non-runnable parent is still listed and is not hidden.
Supplies the second disjunct above: a non-runnable command with at least one available child returns true, so it and its children stay discoverable.
Invoking a non-runnable command aborts with flag.ErrHelp instead of running, which is the source-defined behaviour behind the premise of the question.
ExecuteC turns that ErrHelp into printing the command's own help, which lists its children - i.e. the children are surfaced rather than suppressed.

note: Answer at the pin: no. A command is not made undiscoverable by having a non-runnable parent. IsAvailableCommand() returns true for a non-runnable command that has available subcommands (command.go:1571 with HasAvailableSubCommands), so such a parent is listed under 'Available Commands' and running it returns flag.ErrHelp, which ExecuteC converts into printing that command's help listing its children. Caveat recorded for the reviewer: the word 'deliberately' asks about maintainer intent, which no source span can establish; the spans decide the behavioural half of the question only.

judgements.reason: The condition and mechanism: immediately after ParseFlags, execute() reads the help flag and returns flag.ErrHelp, so the command body, ValidateArgs and all *Run hooks are skipped - --help terminates the command flow here.
ExecuteC intercepts flag.ErrHelp, invokes HelpFunc and returns a nil error, so Execute() hands control back to main with no error - the reason --help does not itself exit the process.
The registration procedure for replacing that default help behaviour (e.g. with one that exits) for a command and its children.
The only process-exit helper Cobra ships; corroborates that exiting is Cobra-adjacent caller code, not part of the help path.

note: Answer at the pin: --help already short-circuits execution - execute() reads the help flag right after ParseFlags and returns flag.ErrHelp before preRun/ValidateArgs/Run, and ExecuteC prints help and returns nil, so Execute() returns to main which then exits normally. To make the help path exit at a chosen point/status, override it with SetHelpFunc (or SetHelpCommand). Both halves are stated by tracked .go bytes at the pin.

judgements.reason: The per-command mechanism: LocalFlags() copies that command's Flags().SortFlags setting onto the local flag set that help/usage renders, so setting it to false on one command disables flag sorting for that command only.

Tracked in-tree corroboration that Flags().SortFlags=false leaves cmd.LocalFlags() unsorted; supporting only - the .go answer span is command.go:1679.

note: Answer at the pin: yes, per command - set cmd.Flags().SortFlags = false (and, for inherited output, the parent's persistent set); command.go:1679 propagates that command's setting into LocalFlags(), which the usage template prints. D4. Cobra implements no conditional-default facility at the pin. Every flag default is supplied once at registration as a single static value - Cobra's own registrations are command.go:1195 (c.Flags().BoolP("help", "h", false, usage)) and command.go:1218/1220 for the version flag - and no tracked .go file computes, re-computes, or overrides a default from a condition; there is no such wording anywhere in site/content/user_guide.md's flag sections (lines 253-366) either. The only source-defined way to tell a supplied value from a default is the pflag Changed bit Cobra reads in ValidateRequiredFlags (command.go:1159); assembling that with the post-parse hook ordering (command.go:888 then 952-973) into a conditional-default recipe would be synthesis the cited bytes do not state. The honest answer is only that Cobra does not provide conditional default values, so no span may be graded 3.

judgements.reason: Names and defines the accessor that yields the complete flag set applying to the command (local plus persistent from itself and all parents) - the entity to enumerate.

Cobra's own in-source procedure for finding which flags were actually supplied on the invocation: take c.Flags(), VisitAll over it, and test each flag's Changed bit (line 1159); this is the operation asked for.
The single-flag variant, climbing the tree to the persistent flag; explains how one named flag is located rather than enumerated.

note: Answer at the pin: enumerate cmd.Flags() (complete set; or LocalFlags()/InheritedFlags() to split it) and, to see which were actually given on the command line, VisitAll over it and test each flag's Changed bit - exactly what Cobra itself does in ValidateRequiredFlags (command.go:1152-1162); cmd.Flag(name) looks up one flag. Note for the reviewer: Q is loosely worded and admits both readings ('which flags apply to this command' and 'which flags did the user pass'); the spans cover both and the answer mode is satisfied under either.

judgements.reason: The deciding mechanism: when resolving the next subcommand, flags and their space-separated values are removed and only non-flag tokens are kept, so flags may sit between the root and the subcommand; conversely the FIRST remaining non-flag token is taken as the subcommand, so a positional arg cannot precede the subcommand name.
innerfind takes argsWOflags[0] as the next subcommand and argsMinusFirstX removes that name while preserving flag values, which is what makes interleaved flags work and stray positional args fatal.

The TraverseChildren path: flags encountered before a subcommand name are collected and parsed against that parent (c.ParseFlags(flags)) before descending, i.e. the source-defined way to have the parent's own local flags accepted between root and subcommand.
The caller-facing switch that selects the Traverse path above.
Tracked documentation of the same condition; supporting evidence only.

note: Answer at the pin: yes for flags, no for positional args. stripFlags() skips flags and their values when locating the next subcommand, so root-level flags may appear before the subcommand name; by default only persistent parent flags are parsed there, and setting TraverseChildren=true makes Cobra parse each parent's local flags via Traverse() before descending. A non-flag token before the subcommand name is instead taken as the subcommand (Find/innerfind on argsWOflags[0]).

Corroborates the alternative of driving the built-in help command programmatically by setting the args to 'help ...' before Execute().

D4. A Cobra Command can belong to exactly one parent: the unexported single-valued field `parent *Command` (command.go:217-218), which AddCommand overwrites unconditionally with `cmds[i].parent = c` (command.go:1308). Handing the same *Command value to two parents therefore leaves it owned by whichever AddCommand ran last, and everything derived from that pointer - CommandPath() (command.go:1426-1434), UseLine() (1437-1451), Root() (861-866), InheritedFlags()/updateParentsPflags() (1696-1718, 1858-1874) - then reports the wrong parent for the other. No tracked .go file at the pin offers shared, linked, aliased-across-parents or re-parented subcommands (aliases at command.go:63-64 are alternative names for one command under one parent, not a second attachment point). The honest answer is only that Cobra does not implement a subcommand shared by several parents, so no span may be graded 3.

D4. The pinned tree generates completion scripts for exactly four shells - bash (bash_completions.go, bash_completionsV2.go), zsh (zsh_completions.go), fish (fish_completions.go) and powershell (powershell_completions.go) - and the default completion command registers exactly those four and no others: completions.go:838 `completionCmd.AddCommand(bash, zsh, fish, powershell)`, with the four subcommands declared at completions.go:713, 748, 787 and 812. There is no cmd.exe / Windows-cmd generator, template, or directive anywhere in the tracked files; the only occurrence of the string `cmd.exe` at the pin is the Windows mousetrap message in cobra.go:74, which is unrelated to completion. PowerShell is a different shell from the Windows cmd shell named in Q, and Q's explicit constraint must be preserved. The honest answer is only that Cobra does not support autocompletion for Windows cmd, so no span may be graded 3.

judgements.reason: The Cobra-provided substitute for reading flag values in a Go init(): register the function here in init(), and Cobra runs it during Execute, after flag parsing.
The essential condition: persistent flag values only exist after ParseFlags runs inside execute(), which is long after package init() has completed - so values cannot be read at init time.
preRun() is where the OnInitialize functions actually run; execute() calls it at command.go:927, i.e. after the ParseFlags above, so those functions do see parsed values.
The set that init() registers persistent flags on (binding a package variable with e.g. StringVar), which is how the value becomes visible later.
How any command later looks a persistent flag up, climbing to the parent that declared it.

note: Answer at the pin: in init() you register the persistent flag on PersistentFlags() (binding a package-level variable), but you cannot read its parsed value there - parsing happens inside execute() at command.go:888, after all init() functions have run. To run initialisation code that does see the values, register it with cobra.OnInitialize; execute() calls preRun() (command.go:927 -> 1015-1019) after ParseFlags. Otherwise read it in PersistentPreRun/PreRun/Run via the bound variable or cmd.Flags().Get*/cmd.Flag(name).

judgements.reason: The exported mechanism for feeding Cobra an argument list of your own instead of the process command line; its doc unit states it replaces the os.Args[1:] default.
The exported entry point that parses a supplied argument slice against the command's merged flag sets - i.e. Cobra's parser is callable directly on your own input.
Shows the condition under which Cobra falls back to the real command line: only when c.args was not set, which is what makes SetArgs effective.
The other exported parsing entry point, resolving a supplied slice to a command plus its remaining args without executing anything.

note: Answer at the pin: yes. Cobra's own parsing entry points are exported and take an argument slice - SetArgs(a) then Execute() runs the whole pipeline on your input (ExecuteC only falls back to os.Args[1:] when c.args is nil, command.go:1076-1081), while Find(args) resolves a command without running it and ParseFlags(args) parses flags only. Constraint recorded: these take []string, so a single string must be tokenised by the caller - Cobra ships no shell-word splitter at the pin.

D4. Cobra implements no watch-like capability at the pin: no tracked .go file contains any polling loop, interval, ticker, timer, refresh or re-execution mechanism (the only time-valued thing in the tree is MousetrapDisplayDuration, cobra.go:77-81, a Windows splash delay). execute() invokes the user's RunE/Run exactly once and returns (command.go:982-988), and ExecuteContext/SetContext (command.go:1027-1033, 264-272) merely carry a caller-owned context. Whether a watch-like CLI exists is therefore wholly a property of the user's own Run body; the affirmative half of any answer would rest on the absence of a constraint rather than on answer-bearing bytes, which A1 and D4 forbid converting into a grade-3 span.

judgements.reason: The mechanism asked for: Context() returns the command's stored context and SetContext replaces it, so a hook can read the context, derive a new one, and store it back for later hooks on the same *Command.
The propagation condition: ExecuteC copies the root's context onto the target command when the target has none, which is what makes one context visible to the hooks that run against that command.
How the initial context is supplied from main; its doc unit states it is retrieved with cmd.Context() inside the *Run lifecycle functions.

judgements.anchor: // PersistentPreRun: children of this command will inherit and execute.
judgements.reason: Fixes the order in which the hooks observe that context (PersistentPreRun, PreRun, Run, PostRun, PersistentPostRun), which the answer's 'between hooks' claim depends on.

note: Answer at the pin: all *Run hooks receive the same *Command, so the context travels on the command itself - in an earlier hook call cmd.SetContext(context.WithValue(cmd.Context(), k, v)) and in a later hook read cmd.Context(). The initial context comes from ExecuteContext/ExecuteContextC or SetContext (ExecuteC defaults a nil ctx to context.Background, command.go:1053-1055) and is propagated to the target command at command.go:1109-1113; the hook ordering is fixed by execute() (command.go:952-1010).

D4. Command.Args is a bare function-typed field (command.go:89-90; type PositionalArgs at args.go:22) and NoArgs is an ordinary package-level function (args.go:41-47) carrying no tag, constant, annotation or wrapper that would identify it once assigned. Grepping every tracked .go file for reads of the field shows Cobra itself never inspects which validator was set: the only tests are the nil checks `if commandFound.Args == nil` (command.go:744) and `if c.Args == nil` (command.go:1140), which distinguish 'unset' (fall back to legacyArgs/ArbitraryArgs) from 'set' and nothing more. No exported accessor or predicate reports the configured validator, and Go function values are not comparable, so the honest answer is only that Cobra provides no way to tell whether NoArgs specifically has been set. Absence must not be converted into a grade-3 span.

D4. Cobra does not preserve or expose the original invocation at the pin. The incoming argv lives only in the unexported field `args []string` (command.go:148-149), for which the tracked tree has a setter (SetArgs, command.go:274-278) and no getter; in ExecuteC the real command line is read into a local variable (`args = os.Args[1:]`, command.go:1076-1081), split by Find/Traverse into a command plus a flag slice, and never retained. What survives parsing is derived material only - CommandPath() (command.go:1426-1434), CalledAs() (1517-1522), UseLine() (1437-1451) and the pflag FlagSet reachable via Flags() - none of which preserves token order, which spelling (long/short/alias) was used, the `=` versus space form, or the position of `--` beyond ArgsLenAtDash (command.go:868-872). No tracked .go file offers an invocation-reconstruction API, so the honest answer is only that Cobra does not implement one; reconstructing an approximation by stitching CommandPath with changed flags would additionally be synthesis the cited bytes do not support.

judgements.reason: The declaration unit for the hook that answers the question: PersistentPreRun/PersistentPreRunE declared on the root is inherited and executed by children, and the documented order puts it before the command's own Run.

The dispatch mechanism: execute() walks from the invoked command up through its parents and runs the first PersistentPreRunE/PersistentPreRun it finds (or, with EnableTraverseRunHooks, all of them root-first), so a single root-level function runs for every subcommand.
The ordering constraint Q asks for - ParseFlags runs first in execute(), so the persistent pre-run hook above sees fully parsed flags.
The alternative: functions registered here run from preRun() (command.go:927, 1015-1019) for every command executed, also after flag parsing, but they receive no *Command or args.
Tracked documentation of the same inheritance and ordering; supporting evidence only.

note: Answer at the pin: declare PersistentPreRun (or PersistentPreRunE) on the root command. execute() parses flags first (command.go:888) and then walks the invoked command's parent chain, running the first persistent pre-run it finds - the root's, unless a subcommand declares its own; set cobra.EnableTraverseRunHooks (cobra.go:64-66) to run every ancestor's hook root-first instead. cobra.OnInitialize is the argument-less alternative, run from preRun() at command.go:927.
